uncited: Pose Recentering transforms a set of camera poses so that their average pose becomes the identity transformation, effectively centering the scene at the origin and aligning the coordinate axes.
This solves the problem of arbitrary camera coordinate systems in Structure-from-Motion (SfM) outputs, which can cause numerical instability and incorrect depth sampling in volume rendering.

It differs from [RotateY](1720-rotatey.md) and [Rotation Transformation](2279-rotation-transformation.md) by simultaneously handling both translation (centering) and rotation (axis alignment) via a single rigid transformation derived from the statistical properties of the pose set, rather than applying fixed or incremental rotations.

**Inputs:** A set of $N$ camera poses, typically stored as an array `poses` of shape $(N, 3, 4)$, where each row $i$ is a $3 \times 4$ matrix $[R_i | t_i]$ representing the world-to-camera or camera-to-world transformation (specifically, camera-to-world $c2w$ in the standard LLFF/NeRF context).
**Outputs:** A recentered set of poses `poses_centered` of shape $(N, 3, 4)$.
The method constructs an average pose matrix $P_{avg}$ that represents the "center" of the camera distribution, then applies the inverse of this matrix to all poses.
Append the row $[0, 0, 0, 1]$ to each of the $N$ poses to create `poses_homo` of shape $(N, 4, 4)$.
Calculate the mean of all translation vectors (the fourth column of the $3 \times 4$ poses, or the last row of the $4 \times 4$ homogeneous poses excluding the last element).
where $t_i$ is the translation part of pose $i$.
In code, this is `poses[..., 3].mean(0)`.
Calculate the mean of all pose z-axes (the third column of the $3 \times 4$ poses, or the third row of the $4 \times 4$ homogeneous poses excluding the last element).
where $r_{i,2}$ is the z-axis vector of pose $i$.
Calculate the mean of all pose y-axes (the second column of the $3 \times 4$ poses).
where $r_{i,1}$ is the y-axis vector of pose $i$.
Compute the normalized cross product of $y'$ and $z$ to ensure orthogonality.
Compute the final y-axis using the cross product of $z$ and $x$ to maintain a right-handed orthonormal basis.
Stack the computed axes and center into a $3 \times 4$ matrix.
Append the row $[0, 0, 0, 1]$ to $P_{avg}$ to create $P_{avg\_homo}$ of shape $(4, 4)$.
Left-multiply the inverse average pose with all homogenized poses.
This results in an array of shape $(N, 4, 4)$.
Remove the last row (the homogeneous row) from each pose.
The method is deterministic based on the input poses.
- **Non-Orthogonal Y-Axis:** The intermediate y-axis $y'$ is not guaranteed to be orthogonal to $z$.
Using $y'$ directly would result in a non-orthonormal basis.
- **Degenerate Scene:** If all cameras are collinear or coplanar in a way that makes the mean z-axis zero or the cross product zero, normalization will fail.
- **Coordinate System Convention:** The method assumes the input poses are camera-to-world ($c2w$).
A variant that transforms poses so that the principal components of the camera positions lie on the XYZ axes.
It recenters the camera positions by subtracting their mean and then computes the eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix of the centered positions.
The eigenvectors are sorted by eigenvalue and assigned to the rotation matrix.
If the determinant of the rotation matrix is negative, the third axis is flipped to ensure a proper rotation.
The transform matrix is constructed by concatenating the rotation matrix and the rotated negative mean position.
A final check flips the y and z axes if the mean z-component of the y-axis of the recentered poses is negative, ensuring a consistent orientation.
- **Time Complexity:** $O(N)$ for computing means and cross products, where $N$ is the number of poses.
The matrix inversion is $O(1)$ for a fixed $4 \times 4$ matrix.
The final transformation is $O(N)$ for matrix multiplication.
- **Memory Complexity:** $O(N)$ to store the input and output poses.
Temporary storage for homogenized poses is also $O(N)$.
- **Measured Performance:** The method is extremely fast, typically taking less than a millisecond for thousands of poses on a modern CPU.
- **Strengths:** Simple to implement, numerically stable for typical SfM outputs, effectively centers the scene for NDC-based rendering.
May not work well for highly non-uniform camera distributions or scenes with large outliers.
